ai_frameworks.title: Compare LangGraph and CrewAI
ai_frameworks.objective: Give a builder an educational, side-by-side view of two popular agent-orchestration frameworks.
plan: Frame the comparison criteria a builder cares about
Collect curated, pre-written evidence cards for each framework
Score each framework on a weighted matrix (Analytics Agent)
Summarize trade-offs and recommend when to pick each

evidence.claim: LangGraph models a workflow as an explicit graph of nodes and edges over a shared, typed state object.
LangGraph supports checkpointing, which enables pausing a run for human input and resuming it later.
CrewAI centres on role-based agents grouped into a crew that works through a list of tasks.
CrewAI's role/goal/backstory abstraction makes quick multi-agent prototypes approachable.
Explicit graphs make control flow easy to inspect and test, at the cost of more upfront design.

findings: LangGraph favours explicit, inspectable control flow — a good fit when you need deterministic routing, approvals and resumable state.
CrewAI favours a higher-level, role-oriented abstraction — a good fit for fast prototyping of collaborative agent teams.
Both can be combined with any model provider; the orchestration choice is largely about how much control-flow visibility you need.
recommendations: Choose LangGraph when you need human-in-the-loop checkpoints, audited routing, or fine-grained state control.
Choose CrewAI when you want to sketch a role-based team quickly and the workflow is mostly sequential.
Prototype the same small workflow in both before committing; framework APIs evolve quickly.
limitations: Educational summary written as a fixture; it is not refreshed from live documentation.
Matrix scores are illustrative opinions, not benchmark results.
Verify current capabilities in each project's official documentation before deciding.

industry.title: Industry snapshot: premium pet-wellness (fictional market)
industry.objective: Sketch a fictional market so you can practice structuring industry research.

evidence.claim: The fictional market is split into nutrition, grooming and wearable health trackers.
In this scenario, subscription nutrition is the fastest-growing segment.
Fictional respondents rank 'vet-approved' as the top purchase driver.

findings: Subscription models dominate the fictional growth story.
Trust signals (vet approval) matter more than price in this scenario.
recommendations: Enter via a niche subscription product with a credible expert partner.
Validate demand with a small pilot before scaling.
limitations: Every number and segment is invented for the demo.
No real companies or markets are described.

fictional_company.title: Company profile: Starlace Robotics (fictional)
fictional_company.objective: Practice a structured company analysis on an invented startup.

evidence.claim: Starlace sells gentle garden-care robots on a monthly lease.
Fictional FY revenue: 4.2M; gross margin: 38%.
Customer churn rose in the last two fictional quarters.

findings: Leasing creates predictable revenue but makes churn costly.
Margin headroom is limited by hardware costs.
recommendations: Explore a service tier to raise margins.

architectures.title: Compare monolith, modular monolith and microservices
architectures.objective: Weigh three architecture styles for a small product team.

evidence.claim: A monolith is simplest to deploy and debug for a small team.
A modular monolith enforces boundaries without distributed-systems overhead.
Microservices enable independent scaling and deployment, at operational cost.

findings: Modular monoliths are a strong default for small teams.
Microservices pay off once teams and scaling needs diverge.
recommendations: Start modular; extract services when a boundary has a clear scaling or ownership reason.
limitations: Scores are illustrative opinions for a fictional team of five.

ai_strategy.title: AI implementation strategies: build, buy or partner
ai_strategy.objective: Compare three ways an organization could adopt AI assistants.

evidence.claim: Buying a packaged tool is fastest but limits customization.
Building in-house maximizes control but needs scarce skills.
Partnering shares risk and accelerates learning.

findings: A phased approach (buy → partner → build) balances speed and control.
recommendations: Start with a governed pilot, measure outcomes, then decide what to build.
limitations: Illustrative scoring for a fictional mid-size company.

insurance_glossary.title: Insurance policy glossary
insurance_glossary.objective: Explain policy terms found in the document in plain language.
plan: Match document terms to glossary cards

evidence.claim: Deductible: the amount you pay before coverage starts paying.
Coverage limit: the maximum the policy pays for a covered loss.
Exclusion: a situation the policy explicitly does not cover.
Premium: the recurring price paid to keep the policy active.

limitations: Glossary is general and educational, not legal or financial advice.
